paras: The white laborers' protest against Black workers on the New York, Ontario and Western Railroad was a labor dispute in Orange County, New York, in August 1881, when Irish and Italian laborers grading the new line threatened to strike over reports that contractors were bringing Black workers from Maryland and the District of Columbia at $1.25 a day. New York and Chicago papers warned of a strike or riot and a protest meeting at Middletown, while correspondents writing from Middletown called the reports exaggerated. No violence was reported, and by August 9 the New-York Tribune declared the trouble over after the contractors disclaimed any present plan to bring more Black workers.

Contractors were grading the railroad that summer, including a twenty-five-mile branch between Cornwall-on-the-Hudson and Middletown, and were short of hands. Most of the force was Italian and Irish, but contractors McLaughlin and Riley had brought Black laborers from Baltimore and Washington in June, 130 by the Tribune's count and about 160 by the Sun's. The Black workers were reported earning $1.25 a day against $1.50 or $1.60 for white men, though contractor Graves said they were paid the same as whites.

On August 5 a rumor spread among the white laborers that a large force of Black workers was on its way from Maryland and the District of Columbia to replace them. According to the New-York Tribune, a contractor's stated intention to bring them on raised such indignation that "a serious strike or a riot" was feared, and the men resolved to meet at Middletown in protest. A New York dispatch to the Chicago Tribune added that one sub-contractor refused to hire Black workers while another vowed to bring them "at all hazards," and that the meeting was set for Sunday, August 7.

On the morning of the meeting the Tribune described the men's feeling as intense and quoted a laborer who said they would quit if Black workers came, calling the plan a scheme to cut their wages. The same report said the Black workers already on the branch did not intend to be frightened by the white men's threats and claimed rights they would "contend for in any emergency." The Sun's Middletown correspondent, however, wrote that no gathering of indignant white laborers would take place, and no report of the meeting's outcome appears in the coverage.

By August 8 the Tribune found things much quieter, with about forty Black workers near Cornwall and contractors promising not to discharge white men. A day later it reported that the contractors had apparently dropped any import plan "on account of the hostility of the Irishmen and Italians to the colored men." A Chicago Tribune dispatch of August 11 instead said the excitement had not abated, work was suspended on some sections north of Cornwall, the directors refused to interfere, and Black workers were still kept on the Middletown branch.

The New-York Tribune broke the story on August 6 under "Opposed to Colored Labor," describing a "threatened invasion of colored labor." The Sun's first item the same day noted that company officers had heard nothing of a strike, and its later Middletown reports called the rumor exaggerated, the August 8 piece presenting "men of various races peacefully working" and quoting a Black worker, through the contractor, in dialect. A wire version treated the dispute as wage competition, portraying the Black workers as "a curious colony" and relaying the white complaint of being "ground down to the level of Italian laborers."

The Salt Lake Herald ran that wire text on August 7, its version of the laborers' complaint using a slur, and the Lake Charles Commercial reprinted the Tribune's "trouble ended" item on August 20 as "Anti-Negro Feeling in New York." The Chicago Tribune alone reported that work had stopped.

Whether a strike was threatened at all is disputed: the two Tribunes reported a feared strike and a protest meeting, while the Sun's Middletown-datelined reports, the closest to the scene, said there was no strike and none was anticipated. The Sun traced the rumor to a change of sub-contractor near Middletown and counted about a hundred Black workers, against first reports of more than 300.

accounts.label: New York and Chicago Tribune reports
accounts.gist: White laborers were inflamed by a planned influx of Black workers at $1.25 a day, called a protest meeting at Middletown, and a strike or riot was feared; the Chicago Tribune later said work was suspended on some sections.

accounts.label: Sun's Middletown correspondents and the contractors
accounts.gist: The strike rumor was exaggerated, arising from a change of sub-contractor; there was no strike, none was anticipated, and no indignation meeting would be held.

accounts.label: Black laborers (as reported by the Tribune)
accounts.gist: The Black workers already employed did not intend to be frightened by the white men's threats and claimed rights they would contend for.

framing.detail: The New-York Tribune headed it 'Opposed to Colored Labor' and spoke of a 'threatened invasion of colored labor', reporting the white laborers' grievance as wage-cutting.
The Sun played down the threat ('Men of Various Races Peacefully Working') and printed the contractor's praise of Black workers alongside dialect quotation of one he called 'Pomp'.
A wire text described the Black workers as 'a curious colony' and relayed the white laborers' complaint about being ground down.
The Chicago Tribune's 'Negro Laborers' and 'Colored Laborers' dispatches stressed predicted and continuing trouble.
